concepts.name: Non-uniform circular motion
concepts.statement: Non-uniform circular motion is circular motion in which the angular velocity changes, as it does for a merry-go-round a child starts from rest or a hard disk that slows to a halt.

concepts.name: Angular acceleration, $\kalpha = \frac{\kdw}{\kdt}$
concepts.statement: Angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity, $\alpha = \Delta\omega / \Delta t$, exactly as linear acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. Its units are radians per second squared, and the faster the angular velocity changes, the greater the angular acceleration.

concepts.name: Tangential acceleration, $\kat = \frac{\kdv}{\kdt}$
concepts.statement: In circular motion the linear acceleration is tangent to the circle at the point of interest, and so it is called tangential acceleration. It is defined as it was for straight-line motion, as the change in the magnitude of the velocity divided by the time taken, and it tells how fast a point on the rim is speeding up or slowing down along its path.

concepts.name: Tangential and centripetal acceleration are perpendicular and independent
concepts.statement: Centripetal acceleration changes the direction of the velocity but not its magnitude, and tangential acceleration changes the magnitude but not the direction. The two are perpendicular to each other, so a body in circular motion may have either, both or neither, and each may be considered on its own.

concepts.name: Tangential and angular acceleration, $\kat = \kr\kalpha$
concepts.statement: Because the radius is constant in circular motion, the change in the linear velocity is the radius times the change in the angular velocity, and so the tangential acceleration is the radius times the angular acceleration. The greater the angular acceleration, the greater the tangential acceleration, and the smaller the wheel, the smaller the tangential acceleration it gives for the same angular acceleration.

concepts.name: Rotational quantities and their translational analogs
concepts.statement: The angle of rotation, the angular velocity and the angular acceleration are the rotational counterparts of position, velocity and acceleration, and each pair is joined by the radius: the angle is the distance divided by the radius, the angular velocity is the velocity divided by the radius, and the angular acceleration is the tangential acceleration divided by the radius. Recognizing the analogy is what lets everything learned about straight-line motion be carried over to rotation.

concepts.name: Change in angular velocity $\kdw$
concepts.statement: The change in angular velocity is the difference between the final and the initial values of the angular velocity.

concepts.name: The rotational kinematic equations, $\kw = \kwo + \kalpha\kt$
concepts.statement: Substituting $v = r\omega$ and $a = r\alpha$ into each of the four kinematic equations for straight-line motion makes the radius cancel, leaving four equations in the angle, the angular velocity, the angular acceleration and the time. They describe the motion without any reference to the forces or masses that produce it, and they hold whenever the angular acceleration is constant.

concepts.name: Average angular velocity, $\kwb = \frac{\kwo + \kw}{2}$
concepts.statement: When the angular acceleration is constant, the average angular velocity is halfway between the initial and the final value, just as the average velocity is halfway between the initial and the final velocity in straight-line motion. The angle turned through is then simply the average angular velocity multiplied by the time.

concepts.name: Linear quantities from angular ones, $\kx = \kr\theta$
concepts.statement: Something spinning in place still carries its rim through a distance, and that distance is the radius times the angle turned through, in radians. In the same way the speed of a point on the rim is the radius times the angular velocity. Radians must always be used in these relationships, and because a radian is dimensionless the product of a length and an angle is a length.

concepts.name: Solving a rotational kinematics problem
concepts.statement: A rotational kinematics problem is solved the way a straight-line one is: check that rotation is involved and that forces and masses need not be, identify the unknown, list what is given, choose the equation that contains the unknown and nothing else unknown, substitute with units, and ask whether the answer is reasonable. Thinking in terms of the translational analog is useful, because that motion is already familiar.

concepts.name: Kinematics of rotational motion
concepts.statement: The kinematics of rotational motion describes the relationships among the rotation angle, angular velocity, angular acceleration and time, without regard to the forces and masses that cause the rotation.

concepts.name: Torque on a point mass, $\ktau = mr^2\kalpha$
concepts.statement: A force applied perpendicular to the radius gives a point mass an acceleration $a = F/m$, and since $a = r\alpha$ this is $F = mr\alpha$. Multiplying both sides by the radius turns the left side into the torque, and the result is the rotational analog of Newton's second law for a single point mass, with $mr^2$ standing where the mass stands in $F = ma$.

concepts.name: Moment of inertia, $\kI = \sum mr^2$
concepts.statement: To rotate anything other than a point mass, the idea of $mr^2$ is extended to a whole body: the moment of inertia is the sum of $mr^2$ over all the point masses of which the body is composed. It plays the part in rotation that mass plays in straight-line motion, it is measured in kilogram meters squared, and because the distance to the axis enters it, a body has a different moment of inertia about every axis.

concepts.name: Moment of inertia depends on how the mass is distributed
concepts.statement: The moment of inertia depends not only on how much mass a body has but on where that mass sits relative to the axis. A merry-go-round full of children is much easier to accelerate when the children stand close to the axis than when they all stand at the rim, although the mass is the same in both cases, because the distance from the axis is squared in every term of the sum.

concepts.name: Newton's second law for rotation, $\text{net}\;\ktau = \kI\kalpha$
concepts.statement: The general relationship among torque, moment of inertia and angular acceleration is that the net torque equals the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration. The larger the torque the larger the angular acceleration, and the larger the moment of inertia the smaller it is. The relationship is valid for any torque, applied to any object, about any axis, which makes it the rotational form of Newton's second law.

concepts.name: Choosing the moment of inertia for a body and an axis
concepts.statement: Calculating a moment of inertia by integration is beyond this text, so the moment of inertia is read from the figure of shapes for the body and the axis at hand: a hoop about its axis, a disk, a rod about its end or about its center, a sphere. Where a system is made of several bodies turning about one axis, the moments of inertia add, since each is a sum of $mr^2$ over the same axis.

concepts.name: Solving a rotational dynamics problem
concepts.statement: A problem in rotational dynamics is set up by determining that torque and mass are involved, choosing the system of interest, drawing a free body diagram of the external forces on it, and applying the rotational form of Newton's second law about the point of rotation, with care taken over which moment of inertia belongs to the body and which axis the torques are taken about. As always, the answer is then checked for reasonableness.

concepts.name: Rotational work, $\text{net}\;\kW = (\text{net}\;\ktau)\theta$
concepts.statement: When a net force is kept perpendicular to the radius of a turning disk, the force is parallel to the displacement and the net work is the force times the arc length travelled. Multiplying and dividing by the radius turns the force into a torque and the arc length into an angle, so that the net work is the net torque times the angle turned through. Torque is analogous to force here, and angle to distance.

concepts.name: Rotational kinetic energy, $\kKErot = \frac{1}{2}\kI\kw^2$
concepts.statement: A body has kinetic energy by turning as well as by travelling, and the rotational kinetic energy is half the moment of inertia times the square of the angular velocity. The expression is exactly analogous to the translational one, with the moment of inertia standing where the mass stands and the angular velocity where the velocity stands.

concepts.name: The work-energy theorem for rotation, $\text{net}\;\kW = \frac{1}{2}\kI\kw^2 - \frac{1}{2}\kI{\kwo}^2$
concepts.statement: Substituting the rotational form of Newton's second law into the expression for rotational work, and then using the kinematic relation between the angular velocity and the angle, gives the net work as the change in one half the moment of inertia times the square of the angular velocity. Net work changes the kinetic energy of a system, and for a turning body that kinetic energy is rotational.

concepts.name: A rolling body divides its energy, $\kPEgrav = \kKEtrans + \kKErot$
concepts.statement: A body rolling down an incline without slipping converts its gravitational potential energy into kinetic energy of two kinds at once, translational and rotational. The greater its moment of inertia, the more of the energy goes into turning and the less is left to carry it down the slope, which is why a can of thick soup, whose contents turn with the can, loses the race to a can of thin soup, and why a can that slides without rolling wins.

concepts.name: Solving a rotational energy problem
concepts.statement: Energy problems that involve rotation are solved as other energy problems are: determine that work or energy is involved, choose the system, decide which kinds of work and energy are present, and for a closed system set the initial kinetic and potential energy equal to the final, remembering that the kinetic energy may have both a translational and a rotational part. For an open system the other forms of energy must be accounted for as well.

concepts.name: Angular momentum, $\kL = \kI\kw$
concepts.statement: Angular momentum is the moment of inertia times the angular velocity, $L = I\omega$, just as linear momentum is the mass times the velocity. Its units are kilogram meters squared per second.

concepts.name: Torque changes angular momentum, $\text{net}\;\ktau = \frac{\kdLang}{\kdt}$
concepts.statement: The net torque on a body is the rate of change of its angular momentum, $\text{net}\;\tau = \Delta L / \Delta t$, which is the rotational form of Newton's second law written in terms of momentum.

concepts.name: Conservation of angular momentum, $\kL = \kLprime$
concepts.statement: If the net torque on a system is zero, then its angular momentum does not change: this is the law of conservation of angular momentum, and it stands beside the conservation of energy and of linear momentum. It is why Earth keeps on spinning, since only the tides exert any significant retarding torque on it, and why a skater can spin for a long time on ice that opposes her very little.

concepts.name: A smaller moment of inertia means a faster spin, $\kI\kw = \kIprime\kwprime$
concepts.statement: Because the angular momentum is conserved when no net torque acts, a body that reduces its moment of inertia must increase its angular velocity to keep the product the same. A skater pulling in her arms and her extended leg spins several times faster, an air mass whose radius narrows becomes a tornado, and the cloud of gas and dust that became the Solar System sped up as gravity drew it together.

concepts.name: Work done in pulling in raises the rotational kinetic energy
concepts.statement: The skater's angular momentum is unchanged when she pulls in her arms, but her rotational kinetic energy rises sharply, and the increase comes from the work she does pulling her arms inward against the force needed to hold them on their circles. Conserving angular momentum does not conserve rotational kinetic energy, because energy can be added from within the system while the angular momentum cannot.

concepts.name: Angular momentum in a collision, $\kL = m\kv r$
concepts.statement: A body moving in a straight line has an angular momentum about any pivot point beside its path, $L = mvr$, where $r$ is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to its line of motion. This is what lets a collision that sets bodies spinning be treated by the conservation of angular momentum.

concepts.name: Solving a collision of extended bodies, $\kwprime = \frac{m\kv r}{\kIprime}$
concepts.statement: A collision in which a body is free to rotate is solved by setting the angular momentum before equal to the angular momentum after, both calculated about the same pivot point. The angular momentum before is that of the incoming body treated as a point mass, and the angular momentum after is the combined moment of inertia about the pivot times the angular velocity, where the combined moment of inertia is the sum of the separate ones about that axis.

concepts.name: Kinetic energy and linear momentum in a rotational collision
concepts.statement: Angular momentum may be conserved in a collision while kinetic energy is not, because the collision is inelastic, and linear momentum need not be conserved either, because the force at the pivot may have a component along the incoming body's path. In the disk and stick the kinetic energy falls from 22.5 J to 1.57 J while the linear momentum rises, which the nail explains: the stick pushes back on the nail and the nail pushes forward on the stick.

concepts.name: The percussion point
concepts.statement: Striking the nailed stick at its far end pushes the nail backward and striking it near the nail pushes the nail forward, so there is a point in between at which no force is delivered to the pivot at all. That point is the percussion point. A tennis racquet and a baseball bat have one too, and a ball met there leaves little force and little vibration in the hand, which is what players call the sweet spot.

concepts.name: The right-hand rule for angular velocity and angular momentum
concepts.statement: Angular velocity and angular momentum are vectors, and their direction is found by curling the fingers of the right hand in the direction of the rotation: the thumb then points along the axis of rotation in the direction of both. Because the angular momentum is the moment of inertia times the angular velocity, and the moment of inertia is a positive number, the two point the same way.

concepts.name: A torque changes angular momentum in its own direction
concepts.statement: The net torque is the rate of change of angular momentum, so the change in angular momentum points the way the torque points. When the torque is perpendicular to the angular momentum already there, the two add head to tail to give a new angular momentum of the same size pointing in a new direction, and the axis of rotation moves perpendicular to the forces applied rather than the way they push.

concepts.name: Gyroscopic precession
concepts.statement: The weight of a spinning gyroscope and the force from its stand create a horizontal torque, always perpendicular to the angular momentum, so the direction of the angular momentum changes while its magnitude does not and the gyroscope precesses about a vertical axis instead of falling over. A gyroscope that is not spinning simply acquires angular momentum in the direction of the torque and falls. Earth precesses in the same way, once in about 26,000 years, under the torque of the Sun and the Moon on its nonspherical shape.

concepts.name: The right-hand rule for rotation
concepts.statement: The right-hand rule defines the directions of angular velocity and angular momentum: when the fingers of the right hand curl in the direction of the rotation, the thumb points in the direction of $\omega$ and of $L$, along the axis of rotation.
